title: Ich bin… Du bist… Sie sind…

situation.setting: Raj arrives at the course office. The teacher, Frau Weber, welcomes him formally.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber
lines.de: Guten Tag! Sind Sie Herr Patel?
lines.en: Good day! Are you Mr Patel?

lines.speaker: Frau Weber
lines.en: Where do you come from, Mr Patel?

lines.speaker: Raj
lines.de: Ja, ein bisschen. Ich spreche Hindi und Englisch.
lines.en: Yes, a little. I speak Hindi and English.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber
lines.de: Anna kommt aus Deutschland. Sie spricht Deutsch.
lines.en: Anna comes from Germany. She speaks German.

grammar.title: The verb sein (to be)
grammar.intro: Sein is the most important verb in German, and it is irregular: you have to learn its forms by heart. Questions that can be answered with yes or no put the verb first.
watchOut: In a yes/no question the verb comes first: Bist du Anna? Sind Sie Herr Patel?
sie (she) and Sie (formal you) look the same at the start of a sentence. Check the verb: Sie ist = she is, Sie sind = you are.
sprechen changes its vowel with du and er/sie: ich spreche, du sprichst, er/sie spricht.

exercises.hint: a question starts with the verb
exercises.explain: Yes/no questions start with the verb: Sind Sie…?
A yes/no question starts with the verb.

exercises.prompt: Match the German with the English.

culture: Address people with Herr or Frau plus their surname: Frau Weber, Herr Patel. Frau is used for every adult woman, married or not. Fräulein is considered outdated. Titles such as Doktor are often added: Herr Doktor Weber.
canDo: I can say who I am and ask someone else with the verb sein.
I can say which languages I speak.
I can ask a yes/no question.
